summary: Arabic joins clauses without changing their word order — there is nothing like the German verb at the end. What changes is the case of what follows. Most linking words are followed by an ordinary clause: وَ (and), أَوْ (or), لٰكِنْ (but), ثُمَّ (then), the prefix فَـ (and so, and then), لِذٰلِكَ (so, therefore), عِنْدَمَا (when), إِذَا (if). A small family, the “sisters of إِنَّ”, must be followed by a noun in the ACCUSATIVE or by a pronoun ending: لٰكِنَّ (but), لِأَنَّ (because), أَنَّ (that) and مَعَ أَنَّ (although) — لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ (because the weather is cold), لِأَنَّهُ مُتْعَبٌ (because he is tired), لِأَنَّنِي جَائِعٌ (because I am hungry). أَنْ (that, to) is followed by a verb in the subjunctive, which ends in -a: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ (I want to go — “I want that I go”, like Greek θέλω να πάω). After إِذَا the verb usually stands in the past form with a present or future meaning (إِذَا جَاءَ الصَّيْفُ نُسَافِرُ), and a command after it needs فَـ: إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا فَكُلْ. In clauses with عِنْدَمَا and إِذَا, “to be” comes back as كَانَ (أَكُونُ, كُنْتَ) with the predicate in the accusative. “When?” in a question is مَتَى, never عِنْدَمَا, and “although …” never takes a “but” in the main clause.

blocks.caption: The pronoun endings are those of the possessives (lesson 6); “I” also لِأَنِّي, أَنِّي, لٰكِنِّي.

blocks.title: The sisters of إِنَّ: subject in the accusative.
blocks.text: لِأَنَّ، أَنَّ، لٰكِنَّ، مَعَ أَنَّ: the next noun is accusative and its predicate nominative — لِأَنَّ الشَّايَ رَخِيصٌ, مَعَ أَنَّ الْمَدْرَسَةَ بَعِيدَةٌ. A pronoun cannot stand alone after them: it becomes an ending — لِأَنَّهُ, never *لِأَنَّ هُوَ.

blocks.title: لٰكِنْ or لٰكِنَّ?
blocks.text: Before a verb or anything else: لٰكِنْ (لٰكِنْ أَذْهَبُ). Before a noun or pronoun as subject: لٰكِنَّ (لٰكِنَّ الشَّايَ رَخِيصٌ, لٰكِنَّهُ جَمِيلٌ). Both mean “but”.

head: person
present (indicative)
after أَنْ (subjunctive)
blocks.caption: أَنْ + subjunctive: -u becomes -a, and the -na of -īna / -ūna falls (the plural keeps a silent alif).

blocks.title: إِذَا + past, and فَـ.
blocks.text: إِذَا ذَهَبْتَ إِلَى السُّوقِ = if you go to the market (past form, future meaning). If the result is a command, a nominal sentence or a negation with لَيْسَ, it begins with فَـ: إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا فَكُلْ! — a present verb needs no فَـ: إِذَا جَاءَ الصَّيْفُ نُسَافِرُ.

blocks.title: “To be” in a time or if clause.
blocks.text: The verbless present cannot follow عِنْدَمَا or إِذَا; use كَانَ with the predicate in the accusative: عِنْدَمَا أَكُونُ مُتْعَبًا (when I am tired), إِذَا كَانَ الْمَطْعَمُ غَالِيًا (if the restaurant is expensive).

blocks.text: وَ adds, فَـ follows at once, ثُمَّ follows later: أَكَلَ وَشَرِبَ (he ate and drank) — جُعْتُ فَأَكَلْتُ (I got hungry, so I ate) — أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ ثُمَّ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ (I drink coffee, then I go to work). The questions “why?” and “when?” are لِمَاذَا and مَتَى; the answers start with لِأَنَّ and عِنْدَمَا.

askYourself: Adding, choosing or contrasting? → وَ, أَوْ, لٰكِنْ / لٰكِنَّ.
Does a noun or pronoun come right after “but / because / that / although”? → لٰكِنَّ / لِأَنَّ / أَنَّ / مَعَ أَنَّ + accusative, or a pronoun ending (لِأَنَّهُ).
Does a verb come right after “but”? → لٰكِنْ.
“That / to” + a verb (want to, must)? → أَنْ + the subjunctive in -a.
A consequence? → لِذٰلِكَ (therefore) or فَـ (and so); one thing after another → ثُمَّ (later) / فَـ (at once).
A time clause → عِنْدَمَا; a question “when?” → مَتَى.
A condition → إِذَا + past form; a command after it → فَـ.
Is there an “is” in the when / if clause? → كَانَ (أَكُونُ, كُنْتَ) + accusative.

traps: *إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا، كُلْ! → إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا فَكُلْ!
*مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ لٰكِنْ أَذْهَبُ → مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ، أَذْهَبُ.

quiz.why: The pronoun becomes an ending on لِأَنَّ; the predicate stays nominative.
Subject accusative after لِأَنَّ, predicate nominative.
أَنْ + subjunctive (-a); أَنَّ is followed by a noun, not a verb.
إِذَا + past of كَانَ + accusative; a command after it takes فَـ.
The question word is مَتَى; عِنْدَمَا only links clauses.

quiz.q: “The house is small, but it is beautiful.”
quiz.why: لٰكِنَّ + pronoun ending; the predicate stays nominative.

quiz.q: “Although I am tired, I go to work.”
options: مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ، أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ، لٰكِنْ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
مَعَ أَنَّ أَنَا مُتْعَبٌ، أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
quiz.answer: مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ، أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
quiz.why: No “but” in the main clause; the pronoun is an ending.

quiz.q: “I drink coffee, then I go to work.”
options: أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ ثُمَّ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ لِأَنَّ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ عِنْدَمَا أَذْهَبَ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
quiz.answer: أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ ثُمَّ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
quiz.why: ثُمَّ = then; لِأَنَّ cannot stand before a verb.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew: אֲבָל (but), כִּי / מִפְּנֵי שֶׁ (because), לָכֵן (so), אַחַר כָּךְ (then), כְּשֶׁ (when), אִם (if), שֶׁ (that), לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ (although) — many end in the prefix שֶׁ, and nothing changes after them: no case, no word order.
German: weil, dass, wenn, obwohl send the verb to the end; deshalb and dann invert (deshalb esse ich). Arabic keeps the order and changes the case after لِأَنَّ / أَنَّ / لٰكِنَّ.
Chinese pairs its linking words: 因为 … 所以 … (because … so), 虽然 … 但是 … (although … but — the pair Arabic does not allow), 如果 …（的话）(if), … 的时候 (when).
The endings on لِأَنَّ / أَنَّ / لٰكِنَّ are the possessive endings of lesson 6 (-ī → -nī for “I”).
After عِنْدَمَا and إِذَا, “to be” returns as كَانَ (أَكُونُ, كُنْتَ) with an accusative predicate.
